title: Spread the letter (2 Kings 19:14–19)
hook: King Hezekiah spreads the threatening letter before God
carry: lay it open before you answer
tomorrow: I have seen thy tears (2 Kings 20:1–6)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hoshea, the last king of the north, and the book of Kings falling silent about the lost tribes. Did a forgotten name come to mind? Today, the empire that took Samaria turns south, toward Jerusalem. Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

A letter arrives. It isn't the first message. Assyria's officer has already stood outside the walls of Jerusalem and shouted, in Hebrew so everyone on the wall could understand: don't let your king fool you. No god of any nation has saved its land from us. Now the king of Assyria, Sennacherib, puts it in writing and sends it to King Hezekiah. Every word is built to make him give up. And Hezekiah does not answer it the way it asks to be answered.
screen: `SHOUTED OUTSIDE THE WALL.` → `NOW IN WRITING.` → `WHAT DOES THE KING DO?`

segments.voice: The text says Hezekiah received the letter from the messengers and read it. Then he went up to the house of the Lord, "and spread it before the LORD." He doesn't answer it. He doesn't tear it up. He doesn't hide it in a drawer and lie awake. He walks it into the Temple and unrolls it, as if to say: here, read this with me. Then he prays, and listen to how the prayer is built. It doesn't start with the threat. It starts with who God is: the God of all the kingdoms of the earth, who made heaven and earth. Only then does he ask: incline your ear and hear, open your eyes and see. See these words, sent to mock the living God. Next, Hezekiah tells the truth about the danger. He doesn't pretend the letter is lying. Yes, he says, the kings of Assyria really have laid waste nations and their lands. They threw their gods into the fire, because those were no gods, only wood and stone made by human hands. The danger is real. He names it plainly. And then the ask: save us out of his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are God. Notice the order: who God is, what's true, what we need. The letter didn't change. The army didn't move. But the king is no longer holding the threat alone in his fist. It's laid open in the house of the Lord. It is a picture of prayer as a page laid out, with nothing hidden. What happens next belongs to another day. Today is just the spreading.
screen: `HE READ IT.` · `SPREAD IT BEFORE THE LORD.` · then, large: `WHO GOD IS, WHAT'S TRUE, WHAT WE NEED.` · then: `NO LONGER HELD ALONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lay one worry down. Sit back and let one breath go. Pick one worry, the one that's been arriving like a letter all week. Picture it as a page in your hands. Now, in your mind, unroll it and lay it flat on a table, so you can see the whole thing. Don't argue with it. Read it honestly: what's true here, and what's only threat? Then leave it there, open, and let your hands rest. If you pray, you can do what Hezekiah did and spread it before God. The bell holds the time.
Hezekiah, who carried Sennacherib's threatening letter into the Temple and spread it open before God instead of holding it alone.
Your line: lay it open before you answer. Today, when a worrying message lands, take one slow breath and lay it open before you answer it. Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Jews read Hezekiah's prayer as part of the book of Kings, and the same story is told again in Isaiah 37; some readers take it as a picture of honest prayer in danger.

original.note: Hebrew: to spread out, the verb used for what Hezekiah did with the letter.

trapdoor: what you thought: a king gets a nasty letter.

notes: Quoted phrase 'and spread it before the LORD' is KJV; JPS 1917 believed identical — please verify.
The officer's speech (2 Kings 18:28–35) is paraphrased and compressed; the speaker is the Rabshakeh.
The line about prayer as a page laid out is the script's own reading, not a cited source.
Root note: פרש 'to spread out' — please confirm vocalization of the dictionary form.
Editor: removed the hook line telling the listener what they would expect; changed 'on the floor of the Temple' (not in the text) to 'in the house of the Lord'.
Audit: 19:14 quotation cited to JPS 1917; fixed garbled 'saved it from us' (18:33 is about each god saving its land); varied templated practice opener.
